plain_english: When I say I do nothing for the sake of pleasure, I'm talking about the wise man — the only person you'll admit is truly capable of enjoying pleasure. But here's my point: I wouldn't call someone wise if they can be overpowered by anything, least of all by pleasure. If a man is consumed by pleasure, how will he stand up to hard work, danger, poverty, and all the troubles that crowd around human life? How will he face the sight of death or endure pain? How will he hold his ground in a chaotic world, fighting off so many relentless enemies, if he's already been beaten by such a soft opponent? He'll do whatever pleasure tells him to do. And do you not see how many things it will tell him to do?
original_excerpt:
When I say that I do nothing for the sake of pleasure, I allude
to that wise man, whom alone you admit to be capable of pleasure:
now I do not call a man wise who is overcome by anything, let alone
by pleasure: yet, if engrossed by pleasure, how will he resist toil,
danger, want, and all the ills which surround and threaten the life
of man? How will he bear the sight of death or of pain? How will
he endure the tumult of the world, and make head against so many
most active foes, if he be conquered by so effeminate an antagonist?
He will do whatever pleasure advises him: well, do you not see how
many things it will advise him to do?

plain_english: "But," our opponent says, "pleasure can't give bad advice when it's paired with virtue." Really? Don't you see what a weak "highest good" that is, if it needs a bodyguard just to keep it good? And how exactly is virtue supposed to rule over pleasure if she's following it? Following is what a subordinate does. Ruling is what a commander does. You're putting the commander in the back of the line. In your philosophy, virtue's grand role is to be pleasure's taste-tester. But we'll see whether virtue can still be called virtue when she's treated with such disrespect. Once she abandons her rightful place, she can no longer keep her rightful name.
original_excerpt:
"It will not," says our
adversary, "be able to give him any bad advice, because it is
combined with virtue." Again, do you not see what a poor kind of
highest good that must be which requires a guardian to ensure its
being good at all? and how is virtue to rule pleasure if she follows
it, seeing that to follow is the duty of a subordinate, to rule
that of a commander? do you put that which commands in the background?
According to your school, virtue has the dignified office of
preliminary taster of pleasures. We shall, however, see whether
virtue still remains virtue among those who treat her with such
contempt, for if she leaves her proper station she can no longer
keep her proper name:

plain_english: But to stay on topic, let me show you how many people are surrounded by pleasures — people Fortune has given everything — and yet you'd have to admit they are miserable. Look at Nomentanus and Apicius, hunting down every delicacy from land and sea, parading the entire animal kingdom across their dinner tables. Watch them lounging on beds of roses, admiring their feast, filling their ears with music, their eyes with shows, their tongues with rare flavors. Their whole bodies are pampered with soft, soothing comforts, and so that even their noses don't go unused, the very room where they worship luxury is thick with perfume. You'd say these people are living the good life. But they are not at ease — because they take pleasure in the wrong things.

in the meanwhile, to keep to the point, I

Fortune has showered all her gifts, whom you must needs admit to
be bad men. Look at Nomentanus and Apicius, who digest all the good

their tables the whole animal kingdom. Look at them as they lie on
beds of roses gloating over their banquet, delighting their ears
with music, their eyes with exhibitions, their palates with flavours:
their whole bodies are titillated with soft and soothing applications,
and lest even their nostrils should be idle, the very place in
which, they solemnize the rites of luxury is scented with various
perfumes. You will say that these men live in the midst of pleasures.
Yet they are ill at ease, because they take pleasure in what is not
good.
